o: De allí a dos días dijo el duque a don Quijote como desde allí a cuatro vendría su contrario, y se presentaría en el campo, armado como caballero, y sustentaría como la doncella mentía por mitad de la barba, y aun por toda la barba entera, si se afirmaba que él le hubiese dado palabra de casamiento.
t: Two days later the duke told Don Quixote that four days after that his opposite would come and present himself in the field, armed as a knight, and would maintain as the damsel lied, halfway through her beard and even with her whole beard, if it were insisted that he had given her his word of marriage.

o: Dejémoslos pasar nosotros, como dejamos pasar otras cosas, y vamos a acompañar a Sancho, que entre alegre y triste venía caminando sobre el rucio a buscar a su amo, cuya compañía le agradaba más que ser gobernador de todas las ínsulas del mundo.
t: Let us let them pass, as we let other things pass, and let us go accompany Sancho, who came trudging along on his donkey, half happy and half sad, in search of his master, whose company pleased him more than being governor of all the isles in the world.

o: Ellos lo recibieron de muy buena gana, y dijeron.
t: They received him very willingly, and said:

o: — No entiendo —respondió Sancho— qué es lo que me pedís, buena gente.
t: "I don't understand," replied Sancho, "what it is you are asking of me, good people."

o: ¿Qué es lo que veo?
t: "What is it I see?"

o: ¿Es posible que tengo en mis brazos al mi caro amigo, al mi buen vecino Sancho Panza?
t: "Is it possible that I hold in my arms my dear friend, my good neighbor Sancho Panza?"

o: Sí tengo, sin duda, porque yo ni duermo, ni estoy ahora borracho.
t: "I do hold him, without a doubt, for I neither sleep nor am I now drunk."

o: Admiróse Sancho de verse nombrar por su nombre y de verse abrazar del estranjero peregrino, y, después de haberle estado mirando sin hablar palabra, con mucha atención, nunca pudo conocerle; pero, viendo su suspensión el peregrino, le dijo.
t: Sancho was astonished to hear himself named and to find himself embraced by the strange pilgrim, and, after having looked at him for a long while without saying a word, with much attention, he could not make him out; but, seeing his perplexity, the pilgrim said to him:

o: — ¿Cómo, y es posible, Sancho Panza hermano, que no conoces a tu vecino Ricote el morisco, tendero de tu lugar?
t: "How is that possible, Sancho Panza, my brother, that you don't know your neighbor Ricote the Moor, the shopkeeper of your town?"

o: Entonces Sancho le miró con más atención y comenzó a rafigurarle, y , finalmente, le vino a conocer de todo punto, y, sin apearse del jumento, le echó los brazos al cuello, y le dijo.
t: Then Sancho looked at him more closely and began to recognize him, and finally he knew him for certain; and, without dismounting from his donkey, he threw his arms around his neck and said:

o: — ¿Quién diablos te había de conocer, Ricote, en ese traje de moharracho que traes?
t: "Who the devil would have known you, Ricote, in that muffler outfit you're wearing?"

o: Dime: ¿quién te ha hecho franchote, y cómo tienes atrevimiento de volver a España, donde si te cogen y conocen tendrás harta mala ventura?
t: Tell me: who made you a Frenchman, and how do you have the audacity to return to Spain, where, if they catch you and recognize you, you will have all the bad luck in the world?

o: — Si tú no me descubres, Sancho —respondió el peregrino—, seguro estoy que en este traje no habrá nadie que me conozca; y apartémonos del camino a aquella alameda que allí parece, donde quieren comer y reposar mis compañeros, y allí comerás con ellos, que son muy apacible gente.
t: "If you don't give me away, Sancho," the pilgrim replied, "I'm sure that in this outfit no one will know me; and let us leave the road for that grove over there, where my companions want to eat and rest, and there you shall eat with them, for they are very peaceable folk."

o: Yo tendré lugar de contarte lo que me ha sucedido después que me partí de nuestro lugar, por obedecer el bando de Su Majestad, que con tanto rigor a los desdichados de mi nación amenazaba, según oíste.
t: I shall have occasion to tell you what has happened to me since I left our town, for obeying the banner of His Majesty, which threatened the wretched of my nation with such severity, as you have heard.

o: Hízolo así Sancho, y, hablando Ricote a los demás peregrinos, se apartaron a la alameda que se parecía, bien desviados del camino real.
t: Sancho did so, and while Ricote was speaking to the other pilgrims they withdrew to the grove that looked like one, well off the royal road.

o: Arrojaron los bordones, quitáronse las mucetas o esclavinas y quedaron en pelota, y todos ellos eran mozos y muy gentileshombres, excepto Ricote, que ya era hombre entrado en años.
t: They threw down their staffs, took off their cloaks or capes, and stripped to the skin, and all of them were young men and very fine gentlemen, except Ricote, who was already a man advanced in years.

o: Todos traían alforjas, y todas, según pareció, venían bien proveídas, a lo menos, de cosas incitativas y que llaman a la sed de dos leguas.
t: They all carried knapsacks, and all of them, as it seemed, were well provided, at least with things that stir the appetite and are said to make a man thirsty two leagues away.

o: Tendiéronse en el suelo, y, haciendo manteles de las yerbas, pusieron sobre ellas pan, sal, cuchillos, nueces, rajas de queso, huesos mondos de jamón, que si no se dejaban mascar, no defendían el ser chupados.
t: They spread themselves out on the ground, and, making tablecloths of the grass, they set upon them bread, salt, knives, walnuts, wedges of cheese, and clean ham bones, which, if they were not chewed, did not deserve to be sucked.

o: Pusieron asimismo un manjar negro que dicen que se llama cavial, y es hecho de huevos de pescados, gran despertador de la colambre.
t: They also set out a black delicacy they say is called caviar, made of fish eggs, a great awakener of thirst.

o: No faltaron aceitunas, aunque secas y sin adobo alguno, pero sabrosas y entretenidas.
t: Olives were not lacking, though dry and with no dressing at all, but tasty and entertaining.

o: Pero lo que más campeó en el campo de aquel banquete fueron seis botas de vino, que cada uno sacó la suya de su alforja; hasta el buen Ricote, que se había transformado de morisco en alemán o en tudesco, sacó la suya, que en grandeza podía competir con las cinco.
t: But what most distinguished that banquet on the field were six wineskins of wine, each of which took his own out of his knapsack; even good Ricote, who had turned from Moor into German or Fleming, brought out his, which in size could compete with the other five.

o: Todo lo miraba Sancho, y de ninguna cosa se dolía; antes, por cumplir con el refrán, que él muy bien sabía, de "cuando a Roma fueres, haz como vieres", pidió a Ricote la bota, y tomó su puntería como los demás, y no con menos gusto que ellos.
t: Sancho watched it all, and was sorry about nothing; on the contrary, to fulfill the proverb he knew very well, that "when you go to Rome, do as you see," he asked Ricote for the wineskin, and took his swig like the others, and with no less relish than they.

o: Cuatro veces dieron lugar las botas para ser empinadas; pero la quinta no fue posible, porque ya estaban más enjutas y secas que un esparto, cosa que puso mustia la alegría que hasta allí habían mostrado.
t: Four times the wineskins were passed around to be tilted; but the fifth time it was not possible, because they were already drier and more parched than esparto grass, a thing that dampened the joy they had shown up to that point.

o: De cuando en cuando, juntaba alguno su mano derecha con la de Sancho, y decía.
t: From time to time, one of them would join his right hand with Sancho's and say:

o: — Español y tudesqui, tuto uno: bon compaño.
t: "Spaniard and Fleming, all one: good fellowship!"

o: Y Sancho respondía: Bon compaño, jura Di!
t: And Sancho would answer: "Good fellowship, by God!"

o: Y disparaba con una risa que le duraba un hora, sin acordarse entonces de nada de lo que le había sucedido en su gobierno; porque sobre el rato y tiempo cuando se come y bebe, poca jurisdición suelen tener los cuidados.
t: And he would burst into a laugh that lasted an hour, not then recalling any of what had happened to him during his governorship; because in the moment and time when one eats and drinks, cares usually have little jurisdiction.

o: Finalmente, con justa razón fuimos castigados con la pena del destierro, blanda y suave al parecer de algunos, pero al nuestro, la más terrible que se nos podía dar.
t: Finally, with good reason, we were punished with the penalty of exile, mild and gentle as it seems to some, but to us the most terrible that could be given to us.

o: Doquiera que estamos lloramos por España, que, en fin, nacimos en ella y es nuestra patria natural; en ninguna parte hallamos el acogimiento que nuestra desventura desea, y en Berbería, y en todas las partes de África, donde esperábamos ser recebidos, acogidos y regalados, allí es donde más nos ofenden y maltratan.
t: Wherever we are, we weep for Spain, for, in short, we were born in it and it is our natural homeland; nowhere do we find the welcome our misfortune longs for, and in Barbary, and in all the parts of Africa, where we expected to be received, welcomed, and feasted, that is where they offend and mistreat us most.

o: Salí, como digo, de nuestro pueblo, entré en Francia, y, aunque allí nos hacían buen acogimiento, quise verlo todo.
t: I left our village, as I say, entered France, and, though there they treated us well, I wanted to see it all.

o: Pasé a Italia y llegué a Alemania, y allí me pareció que se podía vivir con más libertad, porque sus habitadores no miran en muchas delicadezas: cada uno vive como quiere, porque en la mayor parte della se vive con libertad de conciencia.
t: I passed on to Italy and came to Germany, and there it seemed to me that one could live more freely, because its people do not stand on so many niceties: each one lives as he wishes, because for the most part it is lived there with freedom of conscience.

o: Dejé tomada casa en un pueblo junto a Augusta; juntéme con estos peregrinos, que tienen por costumbre de venir a España muchos dellos, cada año, a visitar los santuarios della, que los tienen por sus Indias, y por certísima granjería y conocida ganancia.
t: I took up lodgings in a town near Augsburg; I joined these pilgrims, who make it their custom to come to Spain many of them, every year, to visit its shrines, which they hold to be their Indies, and a most certain and profitable gain.

o: Y lo que me tiene admirado es no saber por qué se fue mi mujer y mi hija antes a Berbería que a Francia, adonde podía vivir como cristiana.»
t: And what fills me with wonder is not knowing why my wife and my daughter went ahead to Barbary rather than to France, where they could live as Christians."

o: A lo que respondió Sancho.
t: To which Sancho replied.

o: — Bien puede ser eso —replicó Ricote—, pero yo sé, Sancho, que no tocaron a mi encierro, porque yo no les descubrí dónde estaba, temeroso de algún desmán; y así, si tú, Sancho, quieres venir conmigo y ayudarme a sacarlo y a encubrirlo, yo te daré docientos escudos, con que podrás remediar tus necesidades, que ya sabes que sé yo que las tienes muchas.
t: "That may well be so," replied Ricote, "but I know, Sancho, that they did not touch my hiding place, because I never revealed to them where it was, fearing some mishap; and so, if you, Sancho, want to come with me and help me take it out and conceal it, I will give you two hundred escudos, with which you may relieve your needs, for you already know that I know you have many."

o: — Y ¿qué oficio es el que has dejado, Sancho? —preguntó Ricote.
t: "And what trade is it you have left, Sancho?" asked Ricote.

o: — He dejado de ser gobernador de una ínsula —respondió Sancho—, y tal, que a buena fee que no hallen otra como ella a tres tirones.
t: "I have left being governor of an island," answered Sancho, "and such an one that, upon my word, they will not find another like it within three leagues."

o: — ¿Y dónde está esa ínsula? —preguntó Ricote.
t: "And where is that island?" asked Ricote.

o: — ¿Adónde? —respondió Sancho—.
t: "Where?" answered Sancho.

o: Dos leguas de aquí, y se llama la ínsula Barataria.
t: Two leagues from here, and it is called the Barataria Island.

o: — Calla, Sancho —dijo Ricote—, que las ínsulas están allá dentro de la mar; que no hay ínsulas en la tierra firme.
t: "Come now, Sancho," said Ricote, "for the islands are out there in the sea; there are no islands on the mainland."

o: — ¿Cómo no? —replicó Sancho—.
t: "How so?" replied Sancho.

o: Dígote, Ricote amigo, que esta mañana me partí della, y ayer estuve en ella gobernando a mi placer, como un sagitario; pero, con todo eso, la he dejado, por parecerme oficio peligroso el de los gobernadores.
t: I tell you, friend Ricote, that this morning I left it, and yesterday I was there governing to my heart's content, like a Sagittarius; but, with all that, I have left it, for it seemed to me a dangerous trade, that of being governor.

o: — Y ¿qué has ganado en el gobierno? —preguntó Ricote.
t: "And what did you gain from the government?" asked Ricote.

o: — He ganado —respondió Sancho— el haber conocido que no soy bueno para gobernar, si no es un hato de ganado, y que las riquezas que se ganan en los tales gobiernos son a costa de perder el descanso y el sueño, y aun el sustento; porque en las ínsulas deben de comer poco los gobernadores, especialmente si tienen médicos que miren por su salud.
t: "I gained," answered Sancho, "the knowledge that I am no fit man for governing, unless it be a herd of cattle, and that the riches that are won in such governments come at the cost of losing rest and sleep, and even one's livelihood; because on the islands governors must eat little, especially if they have doctors who watch over their health."

o: — Yo no te entiendo, Sancho —dijo Ricote—, pero paréceme que todo lo que dices es disparate; que, ¿quién te había de dar a ti ínsulas que gobernases?
t: "I don't understand you, Sancho," said Ricote, "but it seems to me that all you say is nonsense; for who on earth was going to hand you islands to govern?"

o: ¿Faltaban hombres en el mundo más hábiles para gobernadores que tú eres?
t: "Were there ever in the world men more capable of being governors than you are?"

o: Calla, Sancho, y vuelve en ti, y mira si quieres venir conmigo, como te he dicho, a ayudarme a sacar el tesoro que dejé escondido; que en verdad que es tanto, que se puede llamar tesoro, y te daré con que vivas, como te he dicho.
t: "Be quiet, Sancho, and come to your senses, and see whether you want to come with me, as I told you, to help me take out the treasure I left hidden; for in truth it is so great that it may be called a treasure, and I will give you enough to live on, as I have told you."

o: — Ya te he dicho, Ricote —replicó Sancho—, que no quiero; conténtate que por mí no serás descubierto, y prosigue en buena hora tu camino, y déjame seguir el mío; que yo sé que lo bien ganado se pierde, y lo malo, ello y su dueño.
t: "I have already told you, Ricote," replied Sancho, "that I do not want to; be content that as far as I am concerned you will not be discovered, and go on your way in good hour, and let me follow mine; for I know that what is honestly gained is lost, and so is what is ill-gained, along with its owner."

o: — No quiero porfiar, Sancho —dijo Ricote—, pero dime: ¿hallástete en nuestro lugar, cuando se partió dél mi mujer, mi hija y mi cuñado?
t: "I don't want to argue, Sancho," said Ricote, "but tell me: were you in our place when my wife, my daughter, and my brother-in-law left me?"

o: — Sí hallé —respondió Sancho—, y séte decir que salió tu hija tan hermosa que salieron a verla cuantos había en el pueblo, y todos decían que era la más bella criatura del mundo.
t: "I was there," answered Sancho, "and I can tell you that your daughter came out so beautiful that everyone in the village came out to see her, and all of them said she was the most lovely creature in the world."

o: Iba llorando y abrazaba a todas sus amigas y conocidas, y a cuantos llegaban a verla, y a todos pedía la encomendasen a Dios y a Nuestra Señora su madre; y esto, con tanto sentimiento, que a mí me hizo llorar, que no suelo ser muy llorón.
t: She went weeping, and embraced all her friends and acquaintances, and everyone who came to see her, and to all of them she begged they would commend her to God and to Our Lady his mother; and she did this with such feeling that it made me weep, and I am not a great weeper by nature.

o: Y a fee que muchos tuvieron deseo de esconderla y salir a quitársela en el camino; pero el miedo de ir contra el mandado del rey los detuvo.
t: And by my faith, many had a mind to hide her away and set out to take her from them on the road; but the fear of going against the king's command held them back.

o: Principalmente se mostró más apasionado don Pedro Gregorio, aquel mancebo mayorazgo rico que tú conoces, que dicen que la quería mucho, y después que ella se partió, nunca más él ha parecido en nuestro lugar, y todos pensamos que iba tras ella para robarla; pero hasta ahora no se ha sabido nada.
t: Above all, Don Pedro Gregorio showed himself the most passionate, that rich heir youth you know, who they say loved her dearly; and after she left, he has never again appeared in our village, and we all think he has gone after her to steal her away; but up to now nothing has come to light.

o: — Dios lo haga —replicó Sancho—, que a entrambos les estaría mal.
t: "God grant it," replied Sancho, "for it would ill become them both."

o: Y déjame partir de aquí, Ricote amigo, que quiero llegar esta noche adonde está mi señor don Quijote.
t: And let me leave here, friend Ricote, for I mean to reach tonight where my master Don Quixote is.

o: — Dios vaya contigo, Sancho hermano, que ya mis compañeros se rebullen, y también es hora que prosigamos nuestro camino.
t: "God go with you, brother Sancho, for my companions are already stirring, and it is likewise time for us to continue on our way."

o: Y luego se abrazaron los dos, y Sancho subió en su rucio, y Ricote se arrimó a su bordón, y se apartaron.
t: And then the two of them embraced, and Sancho mounted his Dapple, and Ricote took hold of his staff, and they parted.
